title: Feed my sheep (John 21:15–25)
hookLine: three questions for Peter, and a closing line: the world could not hold all the books
tomorrow: To the ends of the earth

lines: I DON'T KNOW HIM, THREE TIMES.
cards: Watch the fires in the last chapters of John. The night Jesus was arrested, Peter stood warming his hands at a charcoal fire in the high priest's courtyard and said three times, I don't know him.
Now it's dawn on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. The disciples have been fishing all night. And on the beach, Jesus has made breakfast, fish and bread, cooking over a charcoal fire.
John uses the same word, charcoal fire, for both. Peter can hardly miss it.

teach.b: After they've eaten, Jesus turns to Peter. Simon son of John, lovest thou me more than these? Yes, Lord, you know I love you.
Feed my lambs. Again: lovest thou me? Yes, Lord.
Tend my sheep. And a third time. John says Peter was grieved, because he asked the third time.
Three denials, three questions. Peter answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, thou knowest all things: thou knowest that I love thee." And Jesus says: "Feed my sheep."
Jesus doesn't make Peter explain the denials or promise never to fail again. He asks one question, about love, and then hands him work.
Each yes becomes a job. In Greek, Jesus uses two different verbs for love, and Peter answers with one of them; scholars still debate how much weight to give that.
What isn't debated is the pattern: the man who failed three times is restored three times, by the same fire.
Catholics see here Peter given the care of the whole flock, part of the foundation of the Pope's office as the shepherd of the Church. Then John ends his Gospel with a shrug of wonder.

teach.h: THE WORLD COULDN'T HOLD THE BOOKS.
teach.b: Jesus did many other things, he says, and if they were all written down, he supposes the world itself couldn't contain the books.

That closes six weeks in John: the Word made flesh, water into wine, Nicodemus at night, the woman at the well, the bread of life, golden lampstands, the good shepherd, Lazarus, the towel, the vine, the cross, and Mary in the garden.
Tomorrow, the story keeps going in a second book.

how: Catholics hear John 21 at Mass in the Easter season, and the Church reads Jesus's charge to Peter as part of the foundation of the papacy; feeding the hungry is one of the works of mercy.

o: a signal fire lit to call the boats ashore
the fire where the Passover lamb was roasted
the fire of Peter's denial, and of his restoring

games.q: the beach at dawn — tap the pairs.
p: where Peter denied him, then breakfast
the world couldn't hold the books

s: Jesus makes Peter explain his denials before forgiving him
he asks only, lovest thou me? and gives him work.
John uses the same word, charcoal fire, at the denial and on the beach
scholars agree the two Greek verbs for love here mean very different things
how much to read into the switch is still debated.

games.q: you're Peter. the man you denied three times has just cooked you breakfast. now he asks a third time, do you love me? what do you say?
o: Lord, thou knowest all things: thou knowest that I love thee.
games.why: grieved, Peter puts it in Jesus's hands: thou knowest all things. Jesus answers, feed my sheep.

practice: Picture a table, a kitchen counter, a bag of groceries, and ask who in your life could use a meal: a neighbor, a coworker eating lunch alone, someone grieving, a kid, a stranger outside the store.

Let one person come clearly to mind, and what you could give them. If you pray, hold Peter's answer, Lord, thou knowest that I love thee, and let the meal be how you say it; if you don't, just hold the person.

wordCard.voice: Charcoal fire. The same word John uses for Peter's denial and for the breakfast fire where Jesus restores him with three questions about love. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: lovest thou me? (John 21:15), Jesus's first question to Peter.

carryVoice: Your line: each yes becomes a job. Love asked three times, and answered with work. Day five hundred thirty-three, done.
